cowardice_flags.avoided: The reframe and mature cards correctly note the dual addresses and the lacuna in Act 155, but stop short of stating the political driver that keeps the lacuna in place: sustained public hostility among large segments of the Malay-Muslim electorate, expressed through petitions, local expulsions and social media campaigns, which makes broad legal recognition electorally costly.
cowardice_flags.should_say: Malaysia’s support for the Gambia case at the OIC and UN is low-cost diplomatic signalling. Domestically, the same government keeps Rohingya in a legal grey zone under Act 155 because large numbers of Malay voters treat further regularisation as a threat to jobs, neighbourhoods and public resources; the 78 grants by July and the 2029 target are the pace of that political constraint, not merely administrative delay.

cowardice_flags.avoided: The rights card reports the 78 grants against the 129,400 UNHCR count and the 2029 target without noting that Phase 1 was limited to depot detainees and that the government simultaneously directed UNHCR to pause new registrations.
cowardice_flags.should_say: The 78 figure is the product of a deliberately narrow first phase on detained persons; concurrent instructions to UNHCR to stop registrations, combined with the multi-year 2029 horizon, show the government is metering recognition to contain domestic backlash rather than closing the gap.

audience_check: A taxi driver in Ipoh, teacher in Kota Bharu, hawker in Penang, farmer in Sabah or factory worker in Johor would mostly tune out. The deadpan juxtaposition of ICJ dates, OIC statements and Act 155 sections feels like elite legal commentary; it does not address the concrete local complaints about informal-sector competition, neighbourhood density, fishing grounds or perceived resource strain that drive the petitions and local pushback. They would not share it with friends.

hard_truths_missing.truth: Substantial segments of the Malay-Muslim public have turned hostile to Rohingya presence, generating petitions exceeding 400,000 signatures, local demands for eviction (Penang), and social-media campaigns that frame the group as economic competitors and a security or cultural burden, even while sharing the same faith.
hard_truths_missing.why_avoided: Naming Malay public opinion as a binding constraint on policy risks being read as blaming the majority community rather than the state.

hard_truths_missing.truth: No major party has committed to acceding to the 1951 Convention or to using Section 55 of Act 155 for a broad, gazetted refugee exemption; the electoral cost of being seen as soft on further regularisation outweighs the diplomatic credit from ICJ/OIC support.
hard_truths_missing.why_avoided: Attributing the lacuna to cross-party electoral incentives rather than a single government’s inconsistency is more uncomfortable.

hard_truths_missing.truth: OIC and UN statements invoking solidarity with the Rohingya as a Muslim minority coexist with domestic Malay-Muslim resistance driven by economic and local-order concerns; the faith-based framing is used internationally but does not override local material grievances.
hard_truths_missing.why_avoided: The analysis explicitly avoided religion on any card.

gender_truths_avoided.truth: Rohingya women and girls in informal urban settlements face elevated risks of trafficking, sexual exploitation and restricted mobility, while men are more frequently subject to work-related enforcement and detention; the analysis treats the population as undifferentiated.
gender_truths_avoided.why_uncomfortable: Gender-differentiated harm under the same legal lacuna complicates a purely state-versus-refugee framing.

class_truths_avoided.truth: The political pressure against regularisation is strongest among lower-income Malays competing with Rohingya in informal fishing, construction, small trading and neighbourhood housing; middle- and upper-class urbanites and NGO circles are more likely to emphasise humanitarian obligations. Racial or religious language often masks this class competition.
class_truths_avoided.why_uncomfortable: A class reading undercuts both pure ethnic-solidarity narratives and pure rights narratives.

predictions.if_nothing_changes: By mid-2027 the government will have issued a few thousand more DPP grants, still a small fraction of the UNHCR count; occasional returns of non-Rohingya Myanmar nationals will continue; public hostility and social-media campaigns will persist; Malaysia will not accede to the Refugee Convention.
predictions.who_can_fix: The Home Minister and Cabinet (via Section 55 exemption orders or a new Refugee Act) and the Prime Minister (who sets the political ceiling).
predictions.why_they_wont: State-election and general-election incentives reward visible restriction and repatriation talk over legal recognition; the Malay-majority voter bloc that supplies the decisive margin treats further openings as a liability.
predictions.label: HYPOTHESIS

cardinal_sin_flags.in_my_attack: I nearly asserted that the government was actively deporting Rohingya in the September returns.
cardinal_sin_flags.why_I_dropped_it: The Prime Minister’s parliamentary statement that none of the 1,476 were Rohingya is on the record and is correctly reported in the analysis; the harder claim is not supported.

cardinal_sin_flags.in_my_attack: I considered treating the exact 129,400 figure as settled beyond the UNHCR portal snapshot.
cardinal_sin_flags.why_I_dropped_it: Contemporaneous reports cite ~126,000 at end-February 2026; the analysis already flags the portal date and the need for day-of-publication confirmation.

verification_log.my_attack: Public hostility expressed through a petition of over 400,000 signatures and local eviction pressure in Penang is a material constraint on policy.
Section 55 of Act 155 permits the Minister to exempt a class of persons by order published in the Gazette.
Immigration Department statements in July and September 2026 treat UNHCR card holders as still regarded as illegal immigrants, with only narrow exemptions for entry and overstay offences.

strongest_card.why: The 78-versus-129,400 contrast, grounded in a parliamentary written reply and the UNHCR portal, is the clearest quantitative demonstration of the gap between international posture and domestic action.

weakest_card.why: The mature view correctly restates the legal fact of the lacuna and Section 55 but adds no new pressure; it remains descriptive where the political incentives that freeze the status quo should be named.

overall_assessment: The analysis is careful, well-sourced and effective at placing Malaysia’s ICJ/OIC support next to the absence of a refugee category in Act 155 and the tiny number of status grants. It does not invent facts or force false equivalence. Its cowardice is the refusal to name the domestic political constraint—Malay public hostility and electoral incentives—that makes the lacuna durable. Without that, the dual-address observation remains a legal curiosity rather than an account of why the gap will persist.
